subject_line: Åmot as medicine in your fifth unincorporated territory book
email_body:
Dear Craig,

I read that the title word of from unincorporated territory [åmot] is the Chamoru word for medicine, and that you meant the experimental and visual poems in this fifth book of the series to offer healing. It made me wonder whether the series has moved from documenting Guam's history toward care.

For a short Spotlight, I would like to ask how you decide when a poem needs to become visual on the page.

subject_line: The Fairy Castle you saw at eight, and From Dust to Stardust
email_body:
Dear Kathleen,

In your Compulsive Reader Q&A you traced From Dust to Stardust back to seeing Colleen Moore's Fairy Castle when you were eight, and you mentioned Mr. Rogers as part of why you care about the people behind objects. I liked a novel growing from a Chicago museum dollhouse into silent-era Hollywood.

For a short Spotlight, I would like to ask how an object leads you to a person, and whether the same thing happened with your earlier historical novels.

subject_line: Walking the Waterville prairie through Restoring Prairie
email_body:
Dear Margaret,

Restoring Prairie asks readers to walk the restored Waterville prairie with you through a full cycle of seasons. It seems a long way from 200 Nights and One Day and the 1967–68 Milwaukee fair housing marches, yet both books are about tending something so it is not lost.

For a short Spotlight, I would like to ask whether you see a link between restoring land and keeping civil rights history alive, and how a single place shapes a whole collection for you.

subject_line: Ten years of listening behind Stringing Rosaries
email_body:
Dear Denise,

Stringing Rosaries began with recording your father and other family members speaking about boarding school, and grew over ten years into sixteen survivor interviews, closing with your own healing journey with your father. The care it took to earn those accounts, many never told even to families, stays with me.

For a short Spotlight, I would like to ask how that listening work has shaped your poetry, and what being North Dakota's Poet Laureate has let you carry into schools.

subject_line: West Texas in the late sixties, in Anything You Recognize
email_body:
Dear Daniel,

The central cycle of Anything You Recognize follows an upwardly mobile family in late-1960s west Texas, with a young boy running up against the era's blurred lines around sex, race and family. Coming ten years after Nights I Dreamed of Hubert Humphrey, it made me curious how a story cycle about one family took shape.

For a short Spotlight, I would like to ask how you decided these stories belonged together, and how running UNM's creative writing program sits alongside your own fiction.

subject_line: Prophet John and the Oak Ridge of Atom City
email_body:
Dear Sara,

Atom City returns to your Manhattan Project hometown of Oak Ridge, and the series about Prophet John, said to have foreseen the bomb a century earlier, sets folk legend beside official history. In your WUOT interview you talked through "But Think, Are You Authorized to Tell It," a title that seems to ask who gets to speak about that legacy at all.

For a short Spotlight, I would like to ask how Oak Ridge looks from Tucson now.

subject_line: From the plants of Rue to the witches of The Witch of Eye
email_body:
Dear Kathryn,

The Monitor in Saint Paul described how the poems in Rue grew out of your research into abortive plants, and your trouble finding specifics about how plants were used in early birth control. The Witch of Eye, published by Sarabande the following year, seems to continue that digging into what was done to women called witches.

For a short Spotlight, I would like to ask how that research moves between poems and essays for you, and what decides which form a discovery takes.
